steps.body: A common denominator is a piece size both fractions can be cut into. Any shared multiple of the two denominators will do.
steps.narration: A common denominator is a piece size both fractions can be cut into. Any shared multiple of the two denominators will do.

widget.successFeedback: 4/12 — the same third, now cut into twelfths so it can meet fourths and sixths.
widget.lowFeedback: That build is SHORTER than 4/12 — either shade more pieces or make each piece larger until the lengths match.
widget.highFeedback: That build is LONGER than 4/12 — either shade fewer pieces or make each piece smaller until the lengths match.

commonFractions.feedback: 1/12 is a single twelfth; a third holds four of them.
3/12 is a quarter, not a third — check what 12 ÷ 3 gives.

predict.prompt: Renaming 1/3 as twelfths, does the amount change?
predict.reveal: Four twelfths cover exactly the ground one third covers; only the cut is finer.

cml.actionGoal: Rename both fractions to the same piece size, then count the pieces for g5u find common.
invariants: Fractions add and subtract only when their pieces are the same size: renaming scales both parts of a fraction and leaves its value untouched, which is what makes g5u find common a counting problem once the denominators agree.
misconceptions: Adding numerators and denominators across, scaling only one part of a fraction when renaming, or forgetting to trade a whole when the top fraction is too small to subtract from.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If only the numerators were made equal instead of the denominators, what would go wrong?

explanationVariants: Multiply to reach the shared size.

commonErrors.feedback: The bottom was multiplied to reach 6, so the top must be multiplied by the same factor.
That subtracted the denominators. Renaming SCALES both parts; it never subtracts.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Give both fractions the same piece size first; after that the pieces simply count.
